optionReasons.saa-med-093:option:2: Forum Store is ephemeral and does not accept volume 'conversion' EBS — the data would be lost in the first stop.

finalJustifications: Because Elastic Volumes changes the type of gp2 to hot gp3 without downtime: ~20% cheaper by GB and baseline of 3.000 IOPS regardless of size.
Because the modification to gp3 migrates data to newer generation disks, and the lower cost comes from hardware efficiency.
Because the gp3 charge only for the effectively used blocks of the volumes, and old fleets have a lot of space allocated without use.
Because the conversion consolidates the fleet's small volumes into shared larger volumes, diluting the cost per instance.

optionReasons.saa-med-094:option:0: Exclude 90 days violates the 5 years — is not optimization, is non-compliance.
optionReasons.saa-med-094:option:1: It's the closest because copying snapshots between regions is a real management operation — but it doesn't save: copying pays for MESMA standard layer in another region (and still the transfer); cutting up 75% has moved the old ones to the EBS Snapshots Archive.
optionReasons.saa-med-094:option:2: Restoring everything in permanent sc1 volumes would multiply the cost — active volumes cost more than snapshots.

finalJustifications: Because EBS Snapshots Archive is the long hold layer: even 75% cheaper than standard, ideal for rarely restored compliance snapshots.
Because the Snapshots Archive compresses the old snapshots in delta format, charging only the modified blocks between months.
Because Snapshots Archive moves snapshots to S3 Glacier account, inheriting the price of cold object archiving.
Because Snapshots Archive disables the collection after the third year of retention, the incentive of AWS for long compliances.

optionReasons.saa-med-097:option:0: It is the closest because it would attack the origin of the problem (new incomplete uploads) — but there is no key to 'disable multipart' in the bucket, and even blocking by policy nothing would remove the already accumulated parts; the lifecycle rule that aborts incomplete uploads clears the past and the future.
optionReasons.saa-med-097:option:1: Versioning does not interact with incomplete multipart parts — only multiplies versions of completed objects.
optionReasons.saa-med-097:option:2: Emptying and re-creating the bucket is destructive and operationally unfeasible — would erase legitimate objects together.

finalJustifications: Because lifecycle rule AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload removes orphan parts after N days — cleans the accumulated and prevents hidden cost from returning permanently.
Because the lifecycle rule automatically concludes incomplete uploads, transforming orphan parts into visible objects.
Because the lifecycle rule compresses the orphan parts in an archiving class, zeroing the cost without erasing the fragments.
Because the lifecycle rule transfers the incomplete parts to a quarantine bucket, where the collection is suspended.

optionReasons.saa-med-098:option:1: The Lambda scale to thousands of concurrent runs in seconds — registration peaks are exactly the strength of the serverless.
optionReasons.saa-med-098:option:2: The costs differ radically according to the standard: high idleness punishes the fixed fleet; high constant volume can favor instances.
optionReasons.saa-med-098:option:3: It's the closest because it starts from a real fact — the Lambda collects per millisecond — but reverses the conclusion: charging for real use is just what ZERA the cost of idleness; the fixed fleet pays the peak sizing 24/7 even empty.

finalJustifications: Because in this profile (rare peaks, long idleness) the serverless collects only the real requests: idleness costs zero, while the fixed fleet pays the peak all the time.
Because the serverless gets the peak discount from AWS, which returns part of the cost of the execution concentrated in short windows.
Because API Gateway absorbs the license plates in the peaks and processes them in batch in the morning, when the price of Lambda is smaller.
Because Lambda reuse the containers of the deactivated fixed fleet, taking advantage of the hardware already paid for during the entire transition.

optionReasons.saa-med-103:option:1: FSx for Windows serves SMB for Windows loads — is not the fit for Linux instances that require POSIX.
optionReasons.saa-med-103:option:2: It's the closest because attaching a shared volume seems to solve — and the EBS multi-attach exists. But it is restricted to volumes io1/io2 NA MESMA AZ and requires own cluster filesystem; simultaneous reading and writing between AZs with POSIX is the drawing of EFS.
optionReasons.saa-med-103:option:3: The s3fs simulates a filesystem over the API Of articles — without semantics POSIX complete or consistent for reliable simultaneous writing.

finalJustifications: Because EFS with mount targets on both AZs delivery POSIX with simultaneous reading and writing for all instances — and survives the fall of a zone.
Because EFS replicates the files to the local disk of each instance of the fleet, and the writings are synchronized between copies.
Because EFS elects an instance as a primary file server, and the others mount the sharing of it via NFS.
Because EFS convert files to objects S3 below, gaining the durability of 11 new in access by file.

optionReasons.saa-med-104:option:0: Lifecycle for Glacier changes storage class by age — does not store overwritten versions or undoes.
optionReasons.saa-med-104:option:1: It's the closest because the CRR it's also real data protection — but it replicates what happens at source: the corrupted version would overwrite the copy too (and without versioning there, nothing returns); recovering previous versions is versioning paper.
optionReasons.saa-med-104:option:3: Weekly manual copy leaves even 7 loss window days and depends on discipline — is not continuous protection.

finalJustifications: Because with Versioning each overwritten creates a new version and preserves the previous one: the corrupted images are reversed by restoring the old version of each object.
Because Versioning validates the content of each upload against the previous version, rejecting corrupted recordings at source.
Because Versioning keeps a trash can 30 days for overwritten objects, restoreable by the support console of the AWS.
Because Versioning replicates versions to a security mirror pocket, untouchable by the catalog application scripts.

optionReasons.saa-med-106:option:1: More instances multiply the synchronous calls that fail — do not keep any request during unavailability.
optionReasons.saa-med-106:option:2: It's the closest because retry with backoff is a real resilience pattern that the AWS — but the requests live in memory of the instance during the attempts: a crash or deployment in the middle loses everything; only the durable row ensures that no request is lost.
optionReasons.saa-med-106:option:3: Multi-AZ no RDS protects the order bank — does not change anything in the synchronous call to the payment service.

finalJustifications: Because the line SQS makes the order durable when it arrives: workers process when payment is standing, and the message only exits the queue successfully confirmed.
Because the line SQS calls the payment service directly, repeating the transactions that fail without involving the instances EC2.
Because the line SQS freezes requests during unavailability and returns them to the application for forwarding as soon as the service returns.
Because the line SQS divides each request between multiple simultaneous workers, and this redundancy eliminates isolated failure loss.

optionReasons.saa-med-108:option:0: It's the closest because it works day by day: a NAT in AZ-A serves the two zones normally — the problem only appears in failure: if AZ-A fall, AZ-B loses the exit together; the isolation requirement requires a NAT by AZ with local route.
optionReasons.saa-med-108:option:1: Internet Gateway on a private sub-network route the public make-up — the instances would be reachable from the internet.
optionReasons.saa-med-108:option:2: One NAT single instance is even more fragile than a NAT Gateway unique: single point of failure, without high availability managed.

finalJustifications: Because one NAT Gateway by AZ with local route eliminates cross-dependence: the failure of NAT of one zone affects only its instances — the other AZ continues with normal output.
'Cause both of you NAT Gateways operate in active-active cluster with shared IP, and traffic migrates alone when one of them falls.
Because the second NAT Gateway fold the available output band, and it is the capacity gap that absorbs the failure of the first.
Because NAT by AZ keeps open connections synchronized between zones, allowing the failure without session drop.
